blocks.text: A steam-turbine generator is run up from rest for the first time. At about a quarter of its running speed the vibration monitor spikes, then settles, and the phase reading flips by half a revolution. Two ideas lie behind this: the rotating force of an off-centre mass, and the critical speed at which the shaft resonates.

blocks.markdown: A rotor is never perfectly balanced. Its mass centre lies a small distance $e$ (m), the eccentricity, from the axis of rotation. Equivalently, an eccentric mass $m_e$ (kg) sits at radius $e$ (m) from the axis. When the rotor spins at angular speed $\omega$ (rad/s), this mass needs a centripetal force $m_ee\omega^2$ (N), supplied by the shaft and bearings. By Newton's third law the bearings feel the same force with the opposite sense, a vector of **constant magnitude that rotates with the shaft**, so it appears as a sinusoidal force at the running speed in any fixed direction.

blocks.title: Unbalance force and critical speed
blocks.text: The unbalance force amplitude is $F=m_ee\omega^2$. The **critical speed** is the shaft speed at which the rotation frequency equals the lateral natural frequency of the rotor: $\omega_c=\sqrt{k/m}$ in rad/s, where $k$ (N/m) is the lateral stiffness of the shaft at the disc and $m$ (kg) is the disc mass (shaft mass neglected). In rpm, $N_c=60\omega_c/(2\pi)$.

blocks.latex: F=m_ee\omega^2,\qquad \omega_c=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}},\qquad k=\frac{48EI}{L^3}\ \text{(simply supported shaft, central disc)}
blocks.caption: Unbalance force; critical speed; central-load stiffness of a simply supported beam, with I = pi d^4/64

blocks.title: Force from an eccentric mass
blocks.prompt: A rotor carries an eccentric mass of 0.02 kg at a radius of 60 mm and runs at 6000 rpm. Find the unbalance force amplitude and compare it with the force at half the speed.

steps.text: At half the speed the force is one quarter, since F is proportional to omega squared.

blocks.answer: F = 474 N at 6000 rpm and 118 N at 3000 rpm.

blocks.markdown: **Whirl of a single disc.** Let the shaft centre $S$ be displaced from the bearing axis by $\mathbf{s}$, and the disc mass centre $G$ be at $\mathbf{s}+e\hat{\mathbf{u}}$, where the unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ rotates at $\omega$ and points from the shaft centre to the heavy spot. Newton's law for $G$, with the shaft spring $k$ and a viscous damping $c$ acting on $S$, is $m\ddot{\mathbf{s}}+c\dot{\mathbf{s}}+k\mathbf{s}=me\omega^2\hat{\mathbf{u}}$. Writing $\mathbf{s}$ as a complex number $s$ and $\hat{\mathbf{u}}=e^{i\omega t}$, try $s=Ae^{i(\omega t-\varphi)}$. Then $A(k-m\omega^2+ic\omega)e^{-i\varphi}=me\omega^2$. Taking magnitudes and the argument gives the results below: the deflection **lags** the heavy-spot direction by $\varphi$.

blocks.caption: Whirl amplitude A (m) and phase lag phi of shaft deflection behind the heavy spot

rows: Shaft deflects towards the heavy spot (heavy spot outside)
Deflection opposes heavy spot; mass centre $G$ moves towards the bearing axis (self-centring)
blocks.caption: Behaviour of a single-disc rotor through the critical speed

blocks.title: Critical speed of a shaft with one disc
blocks.prompt: A steel shaft of diameter 20 mm and length 0.8 m is simply supported at its ends and carries a 6 kg disc at midspan. Take E = 200 GPa and neglect the shaft mass. Find the critical speed in rpm and the whirl amplitude at 3000 rpm for e = 0.1 mm, undamped.

steps.text: Second moment of area of the circular section.
Lateral stiffness at the centre of a simply supported shaft.
Critical angular speed and its rpm equivalent.
At 3000 rpm the speed ratio is r = 314.2/156.7. Undamped, A = e r^2 / |1 - r^2|.

blocks.answer: N_c is about 1496 rpm. At 3000 rpm the speed is 2.01 times critical and the whirl radius is 0.133 mm, only slightly above e (self-centring).

items: Find $m_e e$ (or the mass eccentricity $e$) and the speed $\omega$ in rad/s to get $F=m_ee\omega^2$.
Find the shaft stiffness $k$ at the disc and then $\omega_c=\sqrt{k/m}$; convert to rpm if needed.
Compare running speed with $\omega_c$: below, near, or above the critical speed.
Use $A=er^2/\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}$ for the whirl radius and $\varphi$ for the phase.

blocks.title: Why the phase flips
blocks.text: Below the critical speed the stiffness force dominates and the shaft bends towards the heavy spot. Above it the inertia force dominates and the shaft deflects away from the heavy spot, which means the disc centre of mass settles close to the bearing axis. At resonance, the damping force alone balances the unbalance force, so the lag is $90^\circ$. The phase therefore changes smoothly by nearly $180^\circ$ through the critical speed, which is why the phase lag is a key diagnostic in run-up data.

blocks.title: Critical speed is a natural frequency, not a failure speed
blocks.text: A shaft can run safely above or below its critical speed. Danger arises from lingering near it, because the amplitude is limited only by damping. Practical rotors accelerate quickly through critical speeds, and machines are rarely run within about 10 to 20 per cent of one (typical guidance).

points: Unbalance force is $F=m_ee\omega^2$: constant magnitude, rotating with the shaft, quadrupled when speed is doubled.
The critical speed of a single disc on a shaft is $\omega_c=\sqrt{k/m}$, for a simply supported shaft with central disc $k=48EI/L^3$.
Whirl amplitude $A=er^2/\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}$ peaks near $r=1$ and tends to $e$ at high speed.
The phase lag of deflection behind the heavy spot rises from about $0^\circ$ through $90^\circ$ at the critical speed to nearly $180^\circ$.

questions.stem: An eccentric mass of 0.15 kg sits at a radius of 80 mm on a rotor turning at 900 rpm. Find the amplitude of the unbalance force in newtons.
questions.explanation: The speed is 900 x 2 pi/60 = 94.25 rad/s. The force amplitude is m e omega^2 = 0.15 x 0.08 x 94.25^2 = 106.6 N.

questions.stem: A rotor with a fixed eccentric mass turns at a constant speed. Which statement about the force it exerts on its bearings is correct?

options.text: Its magnitude and direction are both fixed, so it acts like a static load
Its magnitude is proportional to the speed, not its square
It acts along the shaft axis and does not vary with time
Its magnitude is constant and its direction rotates with the shaft, so a fixed sensor sees it as a force at the running frequency

questions.correctOptionText: Its magnitude is constant and its direction rotates with the shaft, so a fixed sensor sees it as a force at the running frequency

distractorRationale.a: The force vector rotates with the heavy spot; a fixed component varies sinusoidally with the shaft.
distractorRationale.b: F = m e omega^2 depends on the square of the speed.
distractorRationale.c: The force is radial (in the plane perpendicular to the axis), not axial.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: The centripetal force required for the eccentric mass has constant magnitude m e omega^2 and always points along the line from the axis to the mass, so it rotates with the shaft.

questions.explanation: The centripetal force required for the eccentric mass has constant magnitude m e omega^2 and always points along the line from the axis to the mass, so it rotates with the shaft. Any fixed-direction component of this force is sinusoidal at the running frequency.

questions.stem: A rotor consists of a 4 kg disc on a shaft that has a lateral stiffness of 2.5 x 10^5 N/m at the disc. Neglecting the shaft mass, find the critical speed in rpm.
questions.explanation: The critical angular speed is sqrt(k/m) = sqrt(62500) = 250.0 rad/s. Multiplying by 60/(2 pi) gives 2387 rpm.

questions.stem: As a lightly damped single-disc rotor is run up from well below to well above its critical speed, the phase of the shaft deflection relative to the heavy spot changes

options.text: from about 0 degrees lag, through 90 degrees at the critical speed, to about 180 degrees lag
from about 180 degrees through 90 degrees to 0 degrees
abruptly from 0 to 90 degrees, with no further change
not at all, because phase depends only on the eccentricity

questions.correctOptionText: from about 0 degrees lag, through 90 degrees at the critical speed, to about 180 degrees lag

distractorRationale.a: Correct: The phase lag satisfies tan(phi) = 2 zeta r/(1 - r^2), so it is near 0 degrees for small r, exactly 90 degrees at r = 1 and approaches 180 degrees for large r.
distractorRationale.b: That is the reverse of the real sequence; at low speed the shaft deflects towards the heavy spot.
distractorRationale.c: The change continues from 90 degrees to about 180 degrees above the critical speed.
distractorRationale.d: Phase depends on the speed ratio and damping, not the eccentricity.

questions.explanation: The phase lag satisfies tan(phi) = 2 zeta r/(1 - r^2), so it is near 0 degrees for small r, exactly 90 degrees at r = 1 and approaches 180 degrees for large r. The shaft deflection therefore ends up opposite to the heavy spot.

questions.stem: A flexible rotor runs at three times its first critical speed with light damping. How does the shaft whirl radius compare with the eccentricity e of the disc mass centre?

options.text: It is many times larger than e
It is slightly larger than e, and the disc tends to rotate about its own mass centre
It is much smaller than e

questions.correctOptionText: It is slightly larger than e, and the disc tends to rotate about its own mass centre

distractorRationale.a: Large amplification occurs only near the critical speed.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: At r = 3, A = e r^2/(r^2 - 1) = e x 9/8 = 1.125 e (undamped).
distractorRationale.c: A = e r^2/(r^2 - 1) is greater than e for every r above 1; it does not drop below e.
distractorRationale.d: Whirl radius tends to e, not to zero; the bearing-axis offset of G is what tends to zero.

questions.explanation: At r = 3, A = e r^2/(r^2 - 1) = e x 9/8 = 1.125 e (undamped). The whirl radius tends to e as r grows, so the mass centre G approaches the bearing axis, a self-centring effect.

questions.stem: A rotor has an eccentricity of 0.2 mm and a damping ratio of 0.05. It runs at 1.25 times its critical speed. Find the steady whirl amplitude in millimetres.

Starting from m s'' + c s' + k s = m e omega^2 exp(i omega t) for the complex displacement s of a disc centre, show how the amplitude and phase of the whirl follow, and explain in physical terms what the phase does as the speed rises through the critical speed.
markingGuide: Try s = A exp(i(omega t - phi)) and substitute
A (k - m omega^2 + i c omega) exp(-i phi) = m e omega^2
Magnitude gives A = m e omega^2 / sqrt((k - m omega^2)^2 + (c omega)^2) = e r^2 / sqrt((1 - r^2)^2 + (2 zeta r)^2)
Argument gives tan(phi) = c omega/(k - m omega^2) = 2 zeta r/(1 - r^2), a lag of the deflection behind the heavy spot
Low speed: phi near 0, stiffness dominates, deflection is towards the heavy spot
At critical speed: phi = 90 degrees, damping balances the unbalance force
High speed: phi tends to 180 degrees, inertia dominates, deflection is opposite to the heavy spot and A tends to e
questions.explanation: The complex equation yields both amplitude and phase in one step. The phase advances through 90 degrees at the critical speed because stiffness dominates below it and inertia above it.

questions.stem: A designer replaces the shaft of a single-disc rotor with one of twice the diameter, same material and length, and the same disc. Neglecting the shaft mass, the critical speed

options.text: increases by a factor of two
increases by a factor of sixteen
increases by a factor of four
stays the same, because the disc mass is unchanged

questions.correctOptionText: increases by a factor of four

distractorRationale.a: Stiffness rises by a factor of 16, and critical speed goes as its square root.
distractorRationale.b: The factor 16 is the stiffness ratio, not the speed ratio.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: The second moment of area scales as d^4, so doubling the diameter multiplies the stiffness k by 16.
distractorRationale.d: Critical speed depends on stiffness as well as mass; stiffness has changed.

questions.explanation: The second moment of area scales as d^4, so doubling the diameter multiplies the stiffness k by 16. Since omega_c = sqrt(k/m), the critical speed rises by sqrt(16) = 4.

questions.stem: A turbine rotor is to run at 4800 rpm and has a first critical speed of 1500 rpm. During run-up the vibration monitor records the amplitude and phase of the 1X (once-per-revolution) component. Describe what the monitor shows as the speed passes 1500 rpm, and explain why the machine is run quickly through that speed and why 4800 rpm is a safe operating point.
markingGuide: Amplitude rises to a peak near 1500 rpm and then falls
Phase lag changes by close to 180 degrees through the peak, passing 90 degrees at the peak
Peak height is 1/(2 zeta) times e, limited by damping
Dwelling near the critical speed allows large amplitudes to build, so run-up should be quick
At 4800 rpm r = 3.2, amplitude A is close to e (self-centring) and well away from resonance
The unbalance force still grows as omega squared, so bearing loads continue to rise even though the whirl amplitude settles
questions.explanation: The run-up data show a resonance peak with a phase swing of nearly half a revolution. At 3.2 times critical the whirl radius is close to the eccentricity.

questions.stem: If both the radius of an eccentric mass and the rotational speed are doubled, the unbalance force is multiplied by eight.
questions.explanation: The unbalance force is m e omega^2, so doubling e doubles the force and doubling omega multiplies it by four. The combined factor is 2 x 4 = 8.
